The pacing of the story feels very balanced and appropriate for the mood it sets. The narrative unfolds largely in "real-time," covering only a few minutes of actual story time from the moment the ferry docks to when Ilse closes it down. However, the author subtly "stretches" these brief moments by weaving in rich sensory details (the smell of mud and iron, the mud on Jonas's shoes, the peeling paint) and internal observations between the sparse lines of dialogue. This slow, deliberate pacing perfectly mirrors the quiet, bleak atmosphere of the November landscape and underscores the unspoken tension and emotional distance between the mother and son. Meanwhile, years of backstory and character development are effortlessly compressed into single sentences—such as contrasting Jonas's childhood spent fishing with his current habit of examining things like spreadsheets, or the mention of the bakery truck changing its route three years ago. This keeps the narrative grounded in the present moment without losing depth.
